description:
Waluigi has assembled this account from field reports, intercepted communication fragments, Bowser's own boastful retelling — which Waluigi has had to deflate by approximately sixty percent to reach plausible truth — and the testimony of several Toads who were present and are still, by all accounts, traumatized. The events described here represent one of the most comprehensive tactical disintegrations Waluigi has ever documented. Not because the enemy was overwhelming, not because the mission parameters changed, but because the party's own decision-making degenerated into a cascade of impulse, stubbornness, and misplaced confidence that scattered them across multiple locations and at least two planes of existence.

Waluigi would like to state for the record: this is what happens when you put a teenager with a gun, a king with abandonment issues, a healer with a savior complex, and a bunch of Toads who think singing solves problems into a hostile supernatural environment and tell them to 'figure it out.'

They figured it out. They figured out how to make everything worse.

## The Locked Room and the Lesson

The incident began in the aftermath of a prisoner situation that Waluigi has documented elsewhere. Markop — the party's healer, moral compass, and increasingly exhausted babysitter — secured a tied-up individual inside a room within Raventree Manor. He shut the door. He locked it. He locked it from his side, which is the kind of deliberate, careful action that suggests Markop had finally begun to understand that leaving loose ends in a haunted manor tends to produce the kind of complications that require stitches.

With the room secured, Green T turned his attention to Remi.

Green T is, in Waluigi's assessment, one of the more competent individuals in this operation. He is not brilliant. He is not powerful. But he pays attention, he thinks before acting, and he has the kind of practical tactical instinct that comes from surviving situations where more talented people died because they were too busy being talented to duck. Green T looked at Remi — a girl who had recently fired a weapon at an ally, missed her intended targets, and displayed the kind of aim that suggests her eyes and her hands have a fundamental disagreement about the location of objects in space — and decided that training was overdue.

'You need to focus better,' Green T told her. His tone, according to witnesses, was not unkind. It was the tone of a man who has accepted that he is going to be teaching someone dangerous how to be dangerous in the correct direction. 'Even if someone pulls you away, you can't miss your shots. What if that was a bad guy?'

The question was rhetorical. The answer was obvious. If it had been a bad guy, Remi would have missed, the bad guy would have not missed, and the Toads would be writing condolence letters.

Green T handed Remi a sheet of paper.

Waluigi has obtained a description of this document. It was a Bros Attack — a cooperative combat technique in which one party member assists another to amplify their effectiveness. The specific technique was a support-fire maneuver: Green T would steady Remi's aim, adjust her positioning, and coordinate timing so that her shots landed with greater force and accuracy. The concept is sound. The execution requires practice, timing, and the kind of mutual trust that is difficult to build when one member of the pair has already shot two people she wasn't supposed to shoot.

The instruction sheet was, by all accounts, a simple childish drawing. Stick figures. Arrows indicating direction of fire. A smiling face next to the word 'GOOD' and a frowning face next to the word 'BAD.' Green T had calibrated his instructional materials to Remi's comprehension level, which Waluigi considers both pragmatic and slightly devastating.

Remi looked at the paper. She understood it. She looked at the locked door.

'I think we should test it on this guy,' she said.

She was referring to the prisoner Markop had just locked in the room.

## The Second Shooting

Markop, who had been organizing supplies, looked up. 'Test what?'

'I got this paper on how to shoot better,' Remi said, holding up the Bros Attack sheet with the enthusiasm of a child showing off a gold star.

'Can I see it?'

She handed Markop the paper. He studied it. The Toads crowded around, staring at the stick-figure diagram with the intensity of military analysts examining battle plans. For a moment, there was the illusion of order — of a team reviewing tactical documentation and preparing a measured response.

Then Markop looked at the locked door. Then he looked at Remi. Then he looked at the door again.

'Toads, guard the door,' Green T said. He gestured to the Toads with the practiced authority of someone accustomed to delegating perimeter security to people whose primary survival strategy is screaming.

'Not on our watch,' the Toads replied, which is a phrase that Waluigi has heard Toads say approximately four hundred times across documented incidents and which has never once prevented the thing they were watching from happening.

Remi aimed at the door.

Markop, displaying the situational awareness that separates him from the rest of this carnival of poor decisions, immediately objected. 'We should not be attacking where a tied-up person is.'

This was correct. This was the reasonable, ethical, tactically sound position. Firing a weapon at a barricaded door behind which a restrained individual was sitting was, by any standard of conduct, a terrible idea.

Salam, meanwhile, was barricading the entrance to their current position. This is the kind of quietly competent action that goes unnoticed when everyone else is arguing about whether to shoot a prisoner through a door. Salam's instinct to fortify rather than attack was correct. Nobody acknowledged it.

Remi aimed. Green T, honoring the spirit of the Bros Attack technique, nudged her aim down slightly. The adjustment was small — a matter of degrees. The difference between 'center mass on a door' and 'lower center mass on a door behind which a person was tied to a chair.'

A shot was fired.

The door broke.

A scream was heard.

Waluigi needs to pause here and perform the kind of controlled breathing exercise that his court-mandated therapist recommended for moments of extreme professional frustration.

Remi shot a tied-up person through a door. This is her SECOND documented firearms offense. The first was the incident in which she fired at someone who turned out to be an ally. The second was firing at a door behind which someone she KNEW was restrained was sitting.

Green T's Bros Attack worked. The shot was more accurate than Remi's unaided fire. The coordination improved her effectiveness. The technique functioned exactly as designed.

It functioned exactly as designed against a PRISONER WHO COULD NOT MOVE.

Markop rushed to the scene. He healed the man. He untied him. He ordered the party to leave the area immediately. The man survived — barely — and was evacuated from the room in a state that Waluigi can only describe as 'justifiably furious at everyone involved.'

Hours passed. The incident settled into the kind of tense silence that follows when everyone in a group knows that something deeply wrong just happened and nobody wants to be the first to address it directly.

Then Markop reached for the gun.

The action was deliberate. Markop extended his hand toward the weapon Remi was carrying. His intent was clear: confiscation. Remi — or more accurately, the FNG, the entity or instinct or whatever mechanism drives Remi's relationship with firearms — resisted. There was a struggle. Hands grabbed at the weapon. For a moment, the party's healer and its most dangerous liability were locked in a physical contest over a gun.

Markop won.

Dan, who had been watching this unfold with the weary expression of a man who has seen too many people make too many bad decisions in too short a timeframe, offered the only appropriate commentary: 'Dang... that was pretty brutal.'

'Remi, you can't use that gun anymore,' Markop said. His voice was firm. The voice of a man drawing a line. 'This is your second time.'

Remi's defense was immediate: 'He pretended to be our friend.'

Markop's response was devastating in its precision: 'Remi, three people have betrayed you. You didn't shoot them.'

Waluigi needs to sit with this exchange. Markop identified the core contradiction in Remi's behavior with surgical accuracy. Remi's stated justification for shooting the prisoner was that he was a traitor — someone who had pretended to be an ally. But Remi had encountered ACTUAL betrayals — three of them, by Markop's count — and had not fired on any of those individuals. The people who genuinely deceived and endangered her received no bullets. The people who were tied up and helpless received gunfire through doors.

Remi was not shooting traitors. Remi was shooting people she COULD shoot. The distinction between 'threat' and 'target' had collapsed in her mind, and the result was that the most vulnerable person in any given situation became her most likely victim.

'They're not betraying me,' Remi said, apparently referring to the three actual traitors. 'They're just having a rough time.'

Waluigi has read this line four times. He has no commentary that would not require language unsuitable for an encyclopedia.

'Those people made this guy pretend to be our friends,' Remi continued, constructing a chain of culpability that absolved the masterminds and condemned the puppet.

'This is impossible,' someone muttered.

Salam, at the perimeter, heard footsteps approaching the barricaded doors.

'We have arrows,' Salam reported.

'We have arrows,' he repeated, his voice carrying the particular emphasis of someone who wants very badly for the people behind him to understand that the tactical situation was evolving and that the time for arguing about gun privileges was OVER.

'Me and my friend,' he added, referring to Eager.

Salam sensed something about the approaching figures. They were undead.

Green T, recognizing that the immediate crisis had shifted from 'internal discipline' to 'external threat,' pivoted back to the Bros Attack training. He showed Remi how to properly hold the gun — if she was going to carry it again, which Markop had not yet authorized but which the situation might require. He showed her how to aim. He put it away.

Remi thought about shooting the undead at the door.

She didn't.

Waluigi considers this the single most significant moment of personal growth Remi has demonstrated in the entire Raventree operation. She had a weapon. She had targets. She had justification. And she chose not to fire. Whether this was because of Green T's training, Markop's confiscation, or simply exhaustion, the result was the same: Remi made a decision that did not involve a bullet.

Waluigi does not know if this represents lasting change or a temporary pause in an escalating pattern. But he documents it because it happened.

## The Moneybags Jungle and the Conflict of Trust

The party moved through what witnesses describe as a section of the manor grounds known informally as the 'Moneybags Jungle' — a dense, overgrown area that Salam found particularly conflicting. The nature of his conflict is not specified in Waluigi's sources, but given Salam's established profile as someone with connections to commerce and a sensitivity to the supernatural, Waluigi suspects the jungle contained elements that triggered both his financial instincts and his survival instincts simultaneously.

They descended to a lower level of the manor. A guard — rushed, breathless, clearly operating under time pressure — intercepted them.

'Oh, Remi! You're just in time for the wedding!'

The guard handed her a paper.

## The Wedding Invitation: A Masterwork of Aristocratic Menace

Waluigi has obtained a copy of this document. He has read it seven times. Each reading has produced a different emotion, ranging from professional admiration for the calligraphy to volcanic fury at its contents. Waluigi will reproduce the relevant sections and provide analysis.

The invitation was issued 'BY DECREE OF THE HOUSE OF VOSS' from 'SUNLESS KEEP, RAVENTREE VALE.' It announced 'A Sacred and Eternal Union' between Remi — identified as 'Ward of the Shadowmere Compact' — and 'Lord Malachar Voss, Third Inheritor of the Onyx Throne, Warden of the Sunless Keep.'

Waluigi needs to address several elements of this document with the seriousness they deserve, because beneath the ornate script and theatrical language lies a legally sophisticated instrument of coercion.

First: Remi is identified as a 'Ward of the Shadowmere Compact.' The word 'ward' is critical. A ward is not a free person. A ward is someone whose legal autonomy has been delegated to a custodial authority. If the Shadowmere Compact holds wardship over Remi, then Remi's consent to the marriage is, under whatever legal framework the Compact operates within, IRRELEVANT. The custodian consents on behalf of the ward. The ward attends.

Second: the phrase 'has waited the appropriate span of mortal decades for the ward to reach her appointed ascendance' is one of the most disturbing sentences Waluigi has read in a career that includes Shroob invasion manuals and Afton research protocols. Lord Voss — an entity old enough to measure time in 'mortal decades' — has been WAITING for Remi to reach a specific age or state. The implication is that this marriage was arranged before Remi was old enough to understand the concept of marriage, possibly before she was born.

'His appetite for this occasion knows no restraint' is a line that Waluigi will not analyze further because his therapist has specifically asked him to avoid dwelling on phrasing that activates what she calls his 'protective rage spiral.'

Third: the guest list is weaponized. Archie Miser is invited as 'Guest of Honor.' Lord Bowser is listed as 'Recognized Dignitary of the Shell Throne.' Green T receives the chilling note: 'Whom We Are Most Delighted to Welcome Back.' Waluigi himself is listed as 'Chronicler of the Recent Unpleasantness.'

The phrase 'Welcome Back' directed at Green T implies prior contact between Green T and the House of Voss. Green T has been here before. Green T has history with these people. The invitation acknowledges this history with the particular warmth of a predator greeting a prey animal that previously escaped.

Fourth: the fine print. Waluigi reproduces the key clause: 'By accepting this invitation the bearer acknowledges the full terms of the Shadowmere Compact (Vol. III, Articles 7-19), waives all rights to magical egress during the ceremony, consents to the temporary suppression of pyromantic faculties within the manor grounds, and agrees that all documentation produced thereafter belongs to the House of Voss in perpetuity. The House of Voss accepts no responsibility for conversions, bindings, or temporal displacements that occur as a natural consequence of attendance. Survival is a courtesy, not a guarantee.'

This is a CONTRACT disguised as an invitation. Accepting it — or even reading it, depending on the magical framework — binds the recipient to terms that include waiving magical escape, suppressing fire abilities, and surrendering intellectual property rights. The casual mention of 'conversions' and 'bindings' as 'natural consequences of attendance' strongly implies that guests at a Voss wedding may be transformed into something other than what they arrived as.

Fifth: the acrostic. The 'verse for the occasion' contains the first letters of each line spelling out a message. Waluigi will not insult the reader's intelligence by pretending this is subtle. The message is a THREAT. Embedded in wedding poetry. Delivered on parchment that dissolves at sunrise.

The final line of the invitation: 'If you are reading this after sunrise, the invitation did not reach you. You were already there.'

Waluigi has encountered many forms of intimidation in his career. This is among the most elegant. The House of Voss has issued an invitation that functions simultaneously as a legal contract, a threat assessment, a guest list of hostages, and a countdown timer. Whoever designed this document understands power, language, and fear with a sophistication that Waluigi finds professionally impressive and personally terrifying.

'This is so sudden,' Remi said.

Waluigi would like it noted that 'this is so sudden' is the most inadequate response to an involuntary marriage summons from an immortal vampire lord that Waluigi can imagine. The appropriate response involves screaming, strategic withdrawal, and ideally a continent between yourself and the Sunless Keep.

## The Evacuation: Markop Takes Command

'Remi, let's go,' Markop said. 'We need to go to the garden.'

This was Markop shifting into emergency mode. The healer had assessed the situation — wedding invitation from a hostile immortal power, party scattered and underequipped, Remi identified as the primary target — and made the only correct tactical decision available: RUN.

'Quickly, Remi. We'll give you a flower.'

'We'll be right there,' Remi said, apparently treating the extraction of her person from an involuntary marriage to a vampire lord with the same urgency as a trip to the market.

Markop offered Salam money to buy arrows. The gesture was practical — Salam needed ammunition, Markop had resources — but Salam's response revealed the depth of trust damage within the party.

'I don't know if I can trust you,' Salam said. 'How do I know it's not a trick?'

Eager agreed: 'Yeah.'

This is what three betrayals, two shootings, one kidnapping invitation, and a general atmosphere of supernatural hostility does to group cohesion. The party's healer offers the party's ranger money for arrows, and the ranger questions whether the money is a trap. The social contract within this group has deteriorated to the point where basic commerce requires trust verification.

Markop did not argue. He did not explain. He picked up Remi.

Physically. He lifted her. Firefighter carry — over one shoulder, her legs secured, her protests muffled against his back. The healer, who had spent the entire operation stitching wounds, managing conflicts, and trying to maintain some semblance of ethical behavior in a situation that punished ethics, simply picked up the girl and started walking.

'We're going,' he said. And they left.

They did not wait for Salam. They did not wait for Eager. They did not wait for anyone. Markop walked out of the building carrying Remi like luggage, his pace steady, his direction clear: away from the wedding, away from the manor interior, toward the garden and the grove beyond it.

Waluigi respects this decision enormously. It was unilateral. It was physically coercive. It was exactly correct. When an immortal vampire lord sends a binding contract disguised as a wedding invitation for someone in your care, you do not hold a committee meeting. You do not consult the stakeholders. You grab the person and you LEAVE.

## The Singing Incident: A Brief and Catastrophic Detour

Outside the manor, voices could be heard in the distance. The party — now partially regrouped, with the Toads following Markop's lead — needed to move through the grounds without attracting attention. People were rolling out a red carpet. With Remi's face on it.

Waluigi needs to repeat that: they were rolling out a RED CARPET with REMI'S FACE on it. The wedding preparations were already underway. The House of Voss was not waiting for RSVP confirmation. They were decorating.

Markop assessed the carpet, assessed the grounds, assessed the distant voices.

'We got to get Remi out of here,' he said.

Bowser, who had apparently been drawn toward the carpet with the instinct of a man who sees ceremonial infrastructure and assumes it might be for him, started heading toward it. A Toad grabbed his arm and redirected him. Bowser, for once, allowed himself to be redirected.

'We should be stealthy,' someone suggested.

Green T asked the Toads if they could start singing.

Waluigi needs to process this sequence. The party identified a stealth requirement. Green T's response to the stealth requirement was to initiate a GROUP MUSICAL PERFORMANCE.

Dan agreed. They sang.

Drums. Loud noises. A full-volume musical number performed by multiple Toads, a plumber in green, and a former ghost-hunting coordinator, all while attempting to sneak past hostile forces that were actively constructing wedding infrastructure for their teammate's involuntary marriage.

Remi sang along. She mumbled the words, still draped over Markop's shoulder, contributing to the chorus with the enthusiasm of someone who has forgotten that she is being carried away from her own kidnapping.

Markop yelled for them to stop.

One by one, they stopped. Dan first. Then Green T. Then the Toads.

Remi kept singing.

She was still in Markop's hands. Still over his shoulder. Still humming, mumbling, half-singing a tune that the rest of the group had abandoned. Markop put his hand over her mouth.

She eventually stopped.

The voices in the distance — the wedding preparation crew, the Voss servants, whoever was rolling out the face-carpet — fell silent. Whether they had heard the singing and were now scanning for its source, or whether they had simply paused in their work, was unclear.

Markop did not wait to find out. He continued moving.

## Tymnas: The Groundskeeper and the Missing Scythe

The party reached the lodge of Tymnas.

Tymnas is, based on available accounts, a groundskeeper responsible for maintaining the grove that serves as the central feature of the Raventree estate's exterior grounds. He is weathered, practical, and possessed of the kind of deep, resigned frustration that belongs to people who have spent their lives performing essential work that nobody respects until it stops getting done.

'How have you been?' Tymnas asked, greeting them with the casual warmth of someone who lives alone in a supernatural forest and treats any visitor as a social event.

He handed them seeds. This detail is noted because Waluigi has learned that in Raventree, nothing is given casually. Seeds from a groundskeeper who tends a supernatural grove may be more than agricultural supplies.

'You wanted some of these siglets, right?' Tymnas asked.

Green T hesitated. 'I don't know. Is that what we need?'

'I'd have to see it first,' someone added.

'Please, come in. Allow my hospitality first,' Tymnas offered.

'We need to see the siglet first,' the party insisted, maintaining at least a veneer of mission focus.

Tymnas showed them his ring finger.

It was on him the whole time.

The siglet — the quest objective they had been pursuing through hours of shooting, singing, fleeing, and involuntary matrimonial documentation — was a ring on the groundskeeper's finger. It had been there the entire time. They could have come straight here.

Waluigi does not know whether to laugh or weep. The party navigated a haunted manor, shot a prisoner, received a vampire wedding invitation, and was nearly discovered by hostile forces, all while the thing they needed was sitting on an old man's hand in a cottage they could have visited first.

'What do you need us to do?' Green T asked.

Tymnas explained. He had been out tending the grove and the tree when an entity — 'the shadowy bastard' — attacked him, sent him sprawling, and stole his staff. His scythe. The tool he used to maintain the grove, to keep the weeds and thorns and darker things in check.

'I use that to kill weeds and thorns,' Tymnas said. 'This grove has a lot of them.'

A tinge of subdued anger leaked through his tone. The anger of a man who has had something essential taken from him and has tried everything within his power to get it back and failed.

'In case it's helpful — no amount of shouting at him will get him to give the scythe back. I've tried.'

Tymnas offered dinner and a bedroom. The door to the guest quarters was blocked.

'Let me get a key,' Tymnas said.

Dan grabbed the doorknob before Tymnas could retrieve the key. Through the door, he heard Bowser whispering.

'Blocking the door — it was him. I made a mess. Give me a bit.'

A pause.

'A king knows how to clean his castle. Give me a bit.'

Waluigi does not know what mess Bowser made in a groundskeeper's guest room, and Waluigi does not want to know. The image of the King of the Koopas frantically tidying a bedroom while whispering through a door like a teenager caught with contraband is, however, permanently filed in Waluigi's memory.

Salam checked outside the window and sensed someone approaching. Dan stepped away from the door and returned the doorknob situation to Bowser's control.

Dan and Tymnas eventually made their way to the bath — a small wooden bucket arrangement that served as the lodge's washing facility. Eager guarded the door. Dan and Tymnas shared the space, apparently comfortable enough with each other to perform the mutual back-rubbing that is either a sign of deep trust or a sign that neither of them has had access to a bath in a very long time.

Eager spoke with Tymnas through the door about the grove's nature.

## The Tree of Woe: Tymnas's Warning

Tymnas described the central feature of the grove with the matter-of-fact dread of someone who has spent years managing something that should not exist.

'There's a grove here which is reflected in shadow,' he explained. 'I was never one for the magic of it all, but it stands the same for the fey and probably the realm you come from as well. Don't know if it's got a name where you're from, but for the fey it's the Tree of Dreams, and for this lot it's the Tree of Woe.'

The Tree of Woe. A tree that exists simultaneously across multiple planes. A tree whose branches, according to Tymnas, were now 'thick with hanging corpses and the blackest crows you ever saw.'

When Tymnas had his scythe, he kept the tree dormant. Sleeping. Under control. Without it, the tree had awakened, and the entity that stole the scythe — the Scorncrow — was using it to enhance its own power rather than maintaining the grove.

'He — it? Y'know what, I'm not sure...' Tymnas paused, seemingly grappling with whether the entity was a person or a thing. He waved the question away. 'Whatever — the Scorncrow's exceptionally dangerous. He uses the scythe's power to enhance its own abilities, rather than tending my damn hedges.'

The Scorncrow was fast, resilient, shrugged off normal weapons, and wielded the stolen scythe with expert proficiency. It commanded a 'giant murder of spectral crows' that obeyed its orders.

Waluigi notes the tactical profile: fast, weapon-resistant, armed with a stolen magical artifact, and commanding aerial spectral forces. This is not a weeding problem. This is a military engagement against a supernatural combatant in its home territory with air superiority.

The party was going to need to fight this thing. With a teenager who just had her gun confiscated, a healer, a couple of Toads, and whatever Bowser was doing in the guest bedroom.

## The Kidnapping: Markop Taken

Time passed. Markop retrieved Eager from the bath — where Eager had been washing Tymnas's body while both of them sat in the small wooden tub, a domestic tableau that Waluigi finds oddly touching in the context of a survival mission in a haunted nightmare grove.

Remi, left momentarily without direct supervision, did what Remi does when unsupervised: she investigated. She explored the kitchen of Tymnas's lodge.

The kitchen was, by all accounts, the warmest and most welcoming space anyone in the party had encountered since arriving in Raventree. Rich yellows and greens — colors that 'practically strained against whatever force sucks the color from this plane.' Shelves of knick-knacks, dishes, foodstuffs. A large circular table. Food that looked 'almost normal.'

Waluigi notes the word 'almost.' In Raventree, even comfort is approximate.

The party heard voices outside — people talking, approaching. The Toads, who were in the bathtub and therefore useless for perimeter security, did not hear them. Tymnas answered a doorbell. Volstos and associates entered the lodge through the front.

The party — Remi, Markop, and whoever else was mobile — slipped out a window as the Voss delegation entered through the front door. They were not seen.

The Toads, apparently oblivious in the bath, picked up a vial of black ash from somewhere in the lodge. This item's significance is unclear but Waluigi documents it because items acquired in Raventree have a tendency to become critical at the worst possible moment.

Markop led the group upward, toward the center of the grove. Toward the place where the scythe was.

He saw someone in the bushes.

'What are you doing?' Markop asked.

The figure — female, humanoid, possibly fey — grabbed his axe.

'Welcome to the grove,' she said. 'Welcome to the gray.'

She grabbed Markop and pulled him into the undergrowth. He disappeared into the grove's interior with the speed and finality of someone being swallowed by vegetation.

Just like that, the party's healer was gone. Kidnapped into a cursed forest by an entity that had also taken his weapon. The person responsible for keeping everyone alive, the person who had just spent the last several hours stitching wounds and confiscating firearms and carrying teenagers away from vampire weddings, was yanked into the bushes like a misplaced garden tool.

Waluigi has seen parties lose their healer before. It never goes well. It goes ESPECIALLY poorly when the healer's absence coincides with an approaching combat encounter against a supernaturally enhanced scarecrow with a stolen scythe.

## The Split: Bowser's Commandeering

Bowser looked at the bushes where Markop had disappeared. 'Are we going to save that guy, or...'

The Toads assessed the situation with the cold pragmatism of people who know their combat limitations. 'Uhh, don't get us wrong, we could, but some of us are fragile.'

Remi offered a perspective that Waluigi finds simultaneously infuriating and emblematic of her entire approach to crisis management: 'He is pretty strong, so he doesn't need help at all.'

Waluigi will note: Markop was just kidnapped. His axe was stolen. He was dragged into a supernatural forest by an unknown entity. And Remi's assessment was 'he'll be fine.'

Bowser offered Remi a comparison that, while crude, contained a kernel of truth that Waluigi finds historically significant: 'You remind me of Peach, if she, uhh, didn't have any guards and was a big baby. At least she would put up a fight.'

'Wow, I can't wait to meet her one day!' Remi said.

Bowser looked down. His expression shifted. Something passed across his face that witnesses describe as sadness — genuine, unguarded sadness, the kind that breaks through even the thickest shell of bravado.

'Right...' he said.

Waluigi documents this moment because it reveals something about Bowser that the King of the Koopas would never willingly expose. Bowser kidnapped Peach dozens of times. Their dynamic was adversarial, obsessive, occasionally theatrical. But in this moment — standing in a haunted grove, looking at a girl who reminded him of someone he would never see again — Bowser mourned.

The party stood there. Nobody was moving toward Markop's rescue. Nobody had a plan.

'I guess we're not planning on helping this guy,' someone observed.

Bowser made a decision. He pointed at Salam.

'YOU! YOUR GOING TO HELP ME! WERE GOING TO LOOK FOR HIM! HE GAVE ME A SOLID! YOUR COMING WITH ME!'

Eager objected immediately: 'Woah, woah, woah — he's our healer! He's coming with us!'

Bowser grabbed Salam. Physically. Lifted him off the ground and held him horizontally, like a surfboard. 'Don't worry, I won't let him get hurt. He is coming with me. He is an accomplice.'

Waluigi is unclear on what Salam was allegedly an accomplice TO, but Bowser's logic was apparently sufficient for Bowser. He held Salam like a surfboard — flat, horizontal, with the kind of grip that suggested the Koopa king had carried things in this configuration before — and walked into the grove.

The party was now in pieces.

Markop: kidnapped, somewhere in the grove, without his axe.

Bowser and Salam (and Dan): heading into the grove to find Markop.

Remi, Eager, and Rodger: alone at the edge of the grove, without a healer, without Bowser's strength, without a plan.

Remi looked at Eager and Rodger. 'The quest is important and we didn't come this way for nothing. So let's do the quest.'

They headed toward the Tree of Woe.

Waluigi documents the party split not because it was strategic — it was the OPPOSITE of strategic — but because it represents the fundamental failure mode of this group. They do not split because of disagreement about objectives. They split because of disagreement about PRIORITIES. Bowser prioritized loyalty — Markop had done him a service, and Bowser repays debts. Remi prioritized the mission — the siglet, the scythe, the tree. Neither was wrong in isolation. Together, they ensured that neither group had sufficient resources to accomplish their goal safely.

## Bowser's Path: The Grove, the Maze, and the Portal

Waluigi now follows Bowser's thread, which is the more violent and ultimately more consequential of the two paths.

Bowser put Salam on the ground. 'YOU LOOK,' he commanded.

Salam found footsteps leading to the right side of the grove. They followed them.

'Why didn't you want to come?' Bowser asked Dan. 'Wasn't he a good help?'

Bowser shouted: 'HEY, YOU! STOP!'

He had spotted something. They continued walking. Then something grabbed Dan.

Dan was pulled into the bushes with tremendous speed and force. One moment he was walking; the next, he was being dragged through the undergrowth by a Mazebound — one of the grove's hostile entities, a creature of the labyrinth that seized intruders and consumed them.

Bowser had one shot.

He roared. He activated his Giant's Might — the ancient magic of his lineage, the power that separates a Koopa king from an ordinary Koopa. He grew. His muscles swelled. His voice shook the trees.

He grabbed Dan.

The Mazebound pulled from the other side.

A tug of war. Dan in the middle. His one arm — Dan has only one arm, a detail that makes this scenario even more nightmarish — was in agony. The Mazebound pulled with the strength of something that lived in the spaces between paths and fed on the lost. Bowser pulled with the strength of a king who had decided that this particular person was HIS to protect.

Bowser roared LOUDER. The sound of it, according to witnesses who were not present but could hear it from across the grove, was like thunder trapped inside a cathedral. He punched with his free fist. Dan tried to dodge — one punch hit him, another hit the Mazebound.

The Mazebound screamed.

Dan slashed at it with whatever weapon he could bring to bear. It screamed again. Bowser tugged harder. The Mazebound tried to grab Bowser's fists. Bowser kept punching.

A fury of punches. The kind of punches Bowser used to smash boulders in his youth, back when the world was simpler and problems could be solved by hitting them hard enough. Each impact drove the Mazebound back. Each roar shook its grip loose.

The Mazebound released Dan. Bowser grabbed him, said 'I'll take this and go,' and RAN.

Waluigi notes: Bowser ran. He did not stay to finish the fight. He did not attempt to kill the Mazebound. He secured the person he came to protect and he LEFT. This is, by Bowser's standards, an extraordinary act of tactical discipline. Bowser's instinct is to fight everything until it stops moving. Choosing retreat — choosing the objective over the battle — suggests that something about this operation has shifted Bowser's priorities in a way that Waluigi finds both encouraging and deeply suspicious.

Bowser continued through the grove. He encountered Bryan the Toad, the original Dan, and the aftermath of a Mazebound engagement.

'YOU! STOP!' Bowser shouted, beheading a Mazebound in passing — apparently unable to sustain his pacifist streak for more than ninety seconds.

'Where is the horse thingy? You know where he is?' Bowser demanded, apparently referring to Markop, possibly referring to a mount, possibly referring to something else entirely. Bowser's communication style under stress tends toward the impressionistic.

The original Dan's eyes glowed. 'Hand over that Dan now.'

'There can only be one,' the original Dan said.

Waluigi needs to address this. There are apparently TWO Dans operating within the party's orbit. The 'original' Dan and a copy, duplicate, imposter, or alternative version. The original Dan's demand — 'hand over that Dan now' — suggests a territorial claim over the identity itself. 'There can only be one' is the statement of someone who considers the existence of a copy to be an existential threat.

Bowser's response was characteristic: 'I don't care about your rivalry or whatever. I just want to know where he is. If you want Dan, ask the other Toads nicely.'

Dan — the copy, the one Bowser had rescued — did not remember the original Dan's name. He did not even recognize him as a version of himself. Whatever process created the duplicate had not included complete memory transfer.

They used fire — non-magical, a simple lighter — to burn through crops blocking their path. They reached the Midnight Portal.

'It's kinda dark,' Bowser said.

The portal lit up.

'Markop went down here,' someone explained.

'How did you save him?' Bowser asked.

Bryan explained: the Mazebound had taken Markop. He started fighting. They told him to run. He ran to the portal and jumped in.

'When you came to us, we were finishing him off,' Bryan said, referring to the Mazebound.

Bowser was not convinced. 'I don't know... I don't even see any footmarks. How do I know you're not lying?'

'Hmm. Well, would we lie to a king?'

'THE KING of the Koopas,' Bowser corrected.

'You really wanted me to leave at first,' Bowser noted.

'Yeah, we were trying to protect you. We didn't know if any other Mazebounds were around.'

'We even got the ingredients here to set up a portal,' they offered.

'How much did you have to get?'

'Four, maybe five. I forget at this point.'

There was a pause. Then, with the casual cruelty of someone who does not understand what they are saying:

'Maybe there's another princess there. Or did you give up on that since she died?'

Silence.

'Don't disrespect the princess,' Bowser said. His voice was different now. Quiet. The kind of quiet that large, powerful beings produce when they are choosing between violence and restraint.

'I kidnapped her many times,' he added. As though that explained everything. As though the history of kidnapping was, in Bowser's mind, a form of devotion rather than a crime.

'Will you ever move on?'

'Is this a therapy session? Back off.'

Waluigi documents this exchange because it is the second time in this operation that Bowser's grief over Peach has surfaced. The first was with Remi. This one is rawer. More defensive. The question 'will you ever move on' hit a nerve that Bowser protects with fury because the alternative is acknowledging the answer.

Bowser ordered them toward the portal. 'Go in there. Prove to me it's safe.'

They looked at each other and nodded. They started walking toward the portal. Bowser, sensing that something was about to go wrong — because something ALWAYS goes wrong — followed. He picked up Dan. He saw them walking. He bumped into them.

The portal activated.

Bowser tripped. He fell in. With Dan.

## The Fracture Atrium: Through the Looking Glass

Bowser and the sleeping Dan materialized in a circular atrium lined with marble statues of Corvinarus ancestors. The faces leaned inward, looming. Intricate teleportation circles of burnished gold were inset within black marble flooring. The sigils that had illuminated upon arrival faded to dull, lifeless gray.

They were in an extraplanar space. A sanctum. Specifically, the receiving area of a sanctum that once belonged to someone named Darius — a wizard, a noble, an entity of sufficient power and ego to construct a personal dimension.

The sigils were dead. The portal behind them was closed. They were trapped.

'Hey, you,' Bowser said, nudging the sleeping Dan. 'Dan, wake up.'

The original Dan — the one who had followed them to the portal — snickered from somewhere in the atrium. 'Great. The original Dan is asleep. All your friends are gone.'

'Where are we?' Bowser demanded.

The original Dan did not answer the question. He approached the sleeping Dan's unconscious body with intent.

Bowser put his hand on the sleeping Dan's shoulder. 'About that — I need you to scram.'

'You in one army?' the original Dan asked.

'I AM my own army,' Bowser replied.

'Fine then. Let's duel over Dan.'

'Alright. Didn't want to do this.'

'This fight will be your last.'

## The Duel: Bowser vs. the Original Dan

What followed was, by Bowser's own account, 'a perfectly fair fight in which I was clearly superior from the start.' Waluigi has adjusted this assessment based on the physical evidence.

The original Dan opened with Scorching Ray — a fire-based magical attack. In any normal environment, this would have been effective. In the Fracture Atrium, magical fire was unstable. The ray backfired, bursting back toward Dan. He shrugged off his own flames — fire resistance, the kind that comes standard with certain mage classifications.

'Ha!' Bowser laughed. 'If you're the real Dan, I feel sorry for the rest to have such a bad copy.'

Bowser cracked his knuckles. 'You showed your fire. How about I show mine?'

Bowser assessed his opponent with a tactical eye that Waluigi would not have credited him with before this operation. He recognized the clothes — Mages' Guild design. Second-class fire mage. Probably trained in the Aumnwood or Ironwood region.

'So you're Mages' Guild, huh? Decently ranked,' Bowser observed.

Dan smiled. 'You gonna breathe some fire or something?'

'Want to talk about your history?'

'Not particularly.'

'Alright. You were a king?'

'Yes. Show me a show only a king could enjoy! Hahahaa!'

Bowser invoked the Fire Rune.

Waluigi must describe this technique because it represents a synthesis of ancient Giant magic and natural Koopa pyromancy that is, from a technical standpoint, genuinely impressive. The Fire Rune is carved into a fist or weapon surface. Upon striking a target, it summons fiery shackles — chains of magma that wrap the victim, restrain them, and burn continuously. The kinetic force of the blow ignites the rune, the rune generates the chains, and the chains cook the target alive.

Bowser's warhammer connected. Twice. Dan was knocked backward with tremendous force, then wrapped in chains of molten fire.

Dan was restrained. The fire shackles held him. But the fire itself had no effect — Dan moved his hands within the burning cuffs as though they were warm bracelets. He continued to smirk.

'Seems like I have this little Toad in my grasp,' Bowser said, misidentifying Dan's species in a way that was probably intentional provocation. 'What was that about being better than me?'

Bowser punched him. 'This is for lying to me.' Black eye.

Another punch. 'This is for acting like you're better than me.' Dan moved his hands. The cuffs broke.

A firestorm descended from above. Dan had summoned it — environmental fire, raining down upon the atrium. Bowser retreated into his shell, weathering the barrage inside his natural armor.

'You got tricks too, huh?' Bowser said, emerging from his shell.

Dan summoned acid elementals. They pierced through Bowser's skin — a new attack vector, not fire but corrosive liquid, bypassing Bowser's heat resistance.

'Huh. Well, you like your little magic, huh?' Bowser said. 'You know what's better than magic?'

He produced a portable Bullet Bill cannon.

Waluigi needs to pause here. Bowser was carrying a PORTABLE BULLET BILL CANNON. Through a haunted grove. Through a midnight portal. Into an extraplanar sanctum. He had it with him THE ENTIRE TIME. He chose to use fists and fire runes for the first portion of the fight because — and Waluigi cannot believe he is writing this — Bowser was showing RESTRAINT.

Two Bullet Bills fired. They tracked Dan with the mindless determination of ordnance designed by Koopa military engineers who believed that the answer to every tactical question was 'more explosions.'

'How do you like my friends?' Bowser laughed.

Dan was hit. 'Then go back home,' he snarled.

'I don't want to be here!' Bowser roared. 'I just want to know where Markop is! You want to be cocky? Act like you're better than me because you're a magic user?'

Bowser laughed — the laugh of a king who has been underestimated for the last time.

'You're acting cocky. Playing dumb. I don't like people who play dumb.'

One final punch. Dan flew backward. He hit a wall. He slid to the floor. Unconscious.

'Look who falls down to the great King Bowser,' the king said, standing over the crumpled body of a second-class fire mage who had made the terminal error of assuming that a large reptile with a crown was merely a large reptile with a crown.

Bowser picked up the cannon. He patted the Bullet Bill affectionately. 'Good job.'

## The Looting: What Bowser Found

Bowser, having incapacitated the original Dan, did what victorious kings do: he searched the body.

The original Dan had a black eye, blue bruising, burn marks, and what Waluigi's medical sources estimate as bruised ribs. He was alive but comprehensively beaten.

Bowser found:

**A photograph.** Dan with other Toads on an airship. With Archie Miser.

'Family reunion, how sweet,' Bowser muttered.

Waluigi needs to address this photograph because it connects the original Dan directly to Archie Miser's operation. Archie has been identified throughout the Raventree crisis as a figure of significant importance — wanted by multiple factions, operating with intelligence resources, and possessing containment knowledge related to the Three-Eyed Bandit. If the original Dan is one of Archie's associates, then his presence in the grove, his demand for the copy Dan, and his willingness to fight Bowser all make strategic sense: he was protecting operational security.

Bowser, of course, did not analyze the photograph strategically. He saw it, filed it under 'leverage,' and kept looking.

**A Mages' Guild notebook.** Containing containment protocols related to the Three-Eyed Bandit.

'This Archie guy is highly wanted, huh?' Bowser mused. 'Maybe if I fight Archie, I can make gold. Friendly fight.'

Waluigi notes that Bowser's instinct upon discovering intelligence about a wanted supernatural entity was to calculate the bounty potential and plan a 'friendly fight' for profit. This is the most Bowser response possible.

**A wand.** Dan's personal casting implement. Bowser took it.

**A water pouch.** Containing Shadeward water — water from the shadow realm itself. Bowser inspected it.

**A gold coin taped to the back of the pouch.** 'Maybe I can pay off Wario's debts,' Bowser thought, which is both mathematically optimistic and morally questionable.

**A Bowser Badge.** This item stopped Bowser cold. Pinned to Dan's body was a badge bearing Bowser's own insignia, with a number written on it: 447.

Bowser stared at it.

He thought about ripping it off.

Skin came off with it.

The badge was not pinned to clothing. It was integrated into Dan's body — fused, bonded, or grown into the skin itself. When Bowser tore it free, Dan's body erupted in flames from the removal point. The badge was not decoration. It was a SYSTEM COMPONENT. Removing it triggered a catastrophic biological response.

Bowser sighed.

'I want information, so I don't want him to die just yet.'

He attempted to reattach the badge. It did not magically rebond. It sat on the torn skin like a ripped piece of clothing — limp, functionless, disconnected from whatever system it had been part of.

Bowser tried to stabilize the wound. He cauterized the torn area — using his own fire breath, presumably, though the method is not specified. The body was stable, but barely. Without proper medical care, the damage would be fatal.

Bowser sighed again. He took the spellbook.

He checked on the sleeping Dan — the copy, the one he had been carrying. Still sleeping peacefully. Bowser searched his pockets. Nothing interesting.

Then Bowser looked up and saw Orange T.

## Orange T and the Collapsing Library

Orange T — a Toad associated with the manor's internal operations — was present in the sanctum, treating Bones. They were in a circular chamber filled with elaborate wooden shelves extending upward in diminishing tiers, packed with leather-bound books. Three grand lecterns stood on a raised platform at the center, holding ornate tomes with metal locks and scrollwork.

The chamber was beautiful. It was also collapsing.

The floor was shattering — slowly, progressively, like fine china hurled in slow motion. The marble broke into fragments. The purple carpet tore and split. The room was being pulled apart by forces that the architecture could not resist.

'WHO ARE YOU?' Bowser shouted. 'ORANGE! THE MANOR GUY!'

Orange T stared.

'Yeah! Come over here!' Bowser yelled.

Waluigi's account of events becomes fragmentary at this point. Bowser is in a collapsing extradimensional library with an unconscious imposter Dan, a sleeping copy Dan, a Toad treating an injured skeleton person named Bones, and no clear way back to the party.

Remi is at the Tree of Woe with Eager and Rodger.

Markop is somewhere in the grove, kidnapped, without his axe.

Salam is in the grove, having been forcibly separated from the group by Bowser and then apparently lost during the portal incident.

Green T's location is unconfirmed.

The wedding is still scheduled.

The scythe is still missing.

The Scorncrow is still active.

The Tree of Woe is still growing corpses.

And the House of Voss is still rolling out a red carpet with Remi's face on it.

## Waluigi's Assessment

Waluigi has documented many operational disasters. The Battle of the Brobot. The Shroob Temporal Incursion. The Fazbear acquisition. Each of those involved extraordinary circumstances — alien invasions, dimensional warfare, haunted pizza robots. Extraordinary circumstances produce extraordinary failures.

The Grove of Woe Incident is not an extraordinary failure. It is an ORDINARY failure amplified by the particular chemistry of this group. Every decision that led to the current catastrophe was individually defensible. Markop locking the prisoner — correct. Green T training Remi — correct. Markop confiscating the gun — correct. Markop carrying Remi away from the wedding — correct. Bowser pursuing Markop's rescue — correct. Remi continuing the mission — correct.

The problem is not that any single decision was wrong. The problem is that correct decisions made by people with incompatible priorities produce INCORRECT outcomes. Markop prioritized protection. Bowser prioritized loyalty. Remi prioritized the mission. Green T prioritized training. Salam prioritized trust verification. Every one of them was right. And the aggregate result of all of them being right was a party scattered across two planes of existence with no healer, no plan, and a vampire wedding approaching.

This is the fundamental paradox of group operations: individual correctness does not guarantee collective success. You can have five people making five good decisions and produce a result that is worse than if one idiot had made all the decisions alone, because at least the idiot would have been CONSISTENT.

Remi needs the scythe. Bowser needs Markop. Markop needs his axe. Salam needs to trust someone. Green T needs to not be 'welcomed back' by vampires. The Toads need to stop singing.

None of these needs are compatible with each other. None of them can be sacrificed without consequence. And the clock — both literal and matrimonial — is ticking.

The wedding invitation said: 'Survival is a courtesy, not a guarantee.'

Waluigi considers this the most honest thing the House of Voss has ever written.

And somewhere in a collapsing library in another dimension, the King of the Koopas is standing over the body of a man he just beat unconscious, holding a photograph that connects to a conspiracy he doesn't understand, in a room full of books he can't read, with a portal that won't reopen behind him.

Bowser's response to this situation will probably involve punching something.

Waluigi is, against his better judgment, rooting for him.

WAH.

summary: Vostolas the Archivist organized a surprise birthday party for Remi. The party contained caged toads, a tanuki disguised as Toadburt, a cake designed to place Remi permanently under Onyx Hand control, and a trapdoor. Disaster Inc. discovered the trap before Remi entered. They extracted the fake Toadburt, exposed him as a tanuki, debated whether to kill him, accidentally shot Eager in the process, argued about slavery as an alternative, watched the democratic process collapse entirely, freed the tanuki into a bathroom anyway, and then Remi was angry that she did not get to cast what she believed should have been the deciding vote on whether to execute the prisoner.
